Source: `analysis/outputs/a2_columns.csv`. The scoring moment is the start of
`snapshot_month`. Decided from the data dictionary's timing note for each
column.

| Decision | Columns | Timing note |
|---|---|---|
| Kept (12) | `tenure_months` | "as of the start of `snapshot_month`" |
| | `sessions_last_30d`, `app_opens_last_30d`, `avg_session_minutes`, `days_since_last_login`, `support_tickets_last_30d`, `referrals_made` | 30 days ending on the last day of the previous month |
| | `payment_failures_last_90d` | 90 days ending on the last day of the previous month |
| | `acquisition_channel`, `city_tier` | fixed at signup |
| | `plan_tier`, `monthly_price` | billing; no timing note. Read as the plan on the billing snapshot at the start of the month. A mid-month change would not be visible, which the dictionary does not rule out. |
| Dropped (2) | `winback_offer_sent` | contact "about this month", from a list circulated on the third business day **after** month close |
| | `exit_survey_started` | the cancellation flow itself; 1 on 1,810 rows, every one a cancellation month, none a non-churner (Exhibit A1 notes) |
| Not features (3) | `member_id`, `snapshot_month`, `signup_month` | identifier; the month (April 2026 is a value never seen in training); redundant with tenure |

## Exhibit A2c — What the row-3 model learned (odds ratios, largest first)

Source: `analysis/outputs/a2_odds_ratios.csv`. Fitted on the building window
only. Numeric columns are standardised inside the pipeline, so "per SD" is
one standard deviation of the building data.

| Feature | Odds ratio | Reading |
|---|---:|---|
| channel = partner_gym / paid_search / organic, vs corporate | 4.3 / 4.1 / 4.1 | a non-corporate member has about 4× the churn odds of a corporate one, all else equal |
| plan_tier = elite vs basic | 0.38 | (collinear with price; read the pair together) |
| sessions_last_30d | 0.57 per SD; 0.88 per session | each extra session cuts churn odds 12% |
| avg_session_minutes | 0.61 per SD | |
| monthly_price | 1.38 per SD | |
| days_since_last_login | 1.33 per SD | |
| tenure_months | 0.85 per SD | weak, as in Exhibit A1 |
| everything else | 0.9 – 1.1 | near nothing |

---

## Prose (final draft for §1 A2, session 3; 552 words, trim after A3)

**Order.** Columns first, folds second, time third, segment last. Two facts
fix most of it. Once the evaluation is past-to-future there are no folds left
to group, so change 2 has to precede change 3 or it measures nothing by
construction. And change 3 is the row that touches the test window, so it
comes as late as possible, and row 4 splits the same scores rather than
scoring again. Change 1 goes first because it is the one change to the data
rather than to the protocol: every row after it is measured on a model that
could actually be deployed.

**Reading the rows.** Row 0: deduplication and restricting to the building
window leave the number where it was; the leak dominates everything else.
Row 1: removing the two columns recorded after the scoring moment costs 0.22,
which is the size of what the analyst's model was reading off the
cancellation itself. Row 2: under the analyst's random split, 2,899 of 3,648
members (79.5%) have rows in two or more folds; grouping removes all of that
overlap and the number moves by 0.001, because the twelve admissible columns
contain nothing that identifies a member and a linear model cannot
manufacture identity out of shared attributes. The change was still right;
a more flexible model would have paid for it. Row 3: rows 0 to 2 were
already scored on data the fitting model had not seen. What changes here is
that the unseen data is *later*, and a model fit through June 2025 ranks
October to December at 0.644. The 0.10 is the cost of time, not of novelty.
Row 4: the same scores, split by channel. Corporate members, 860 rows and 34
churners, are ranked at 0.404, below a coin flip; everyone else at 0.641,
which is also the pooled number, since corporate is 19% of test rows but 8%
of test churners. The model's largest single term is the channel itself,
about four times the churn odds for any non-corporate channel (Exhibit A2c),
learned from 533 corporate rows with at most six months of tenure. Within the
segment its behavioural columns rank the wrong way.

**Why the rows do not decompose.** Each row measures its change on top of
the rows above it, so the differences sum to the total but the split depends
on the path. `exit_survey_started` is 1 on every churner's last row in every
period. Had past-to-future been done first with that column still in, the
test AUC would have stayed near 0.97 and time would have looked free;
dropping the columns afterwards would then have taken the whole fall,
including the 0.10 attributed here to time. Same total, different split.

**The two-month gap.** A June 2025 row's label is fixed by whether the member
cancels by 31 August 2025, so training labels encode July and August
outcomes; the gap ends training at the last month whose labels have matured
before validation starts. It also mirrors deployment: on 1 April 2026 the
two most recent months of labels will not exist either.

**Columns.** Exhibit A2b argues each of the fourteen from the dictionary's
timing note, kept and dropped alike. The one reading rather than a fact:
`plan_tier` and `monthly_price` carry no timing note and are taken as the
billing snapshot at the start of the month.

---

## Notes to self (not memo text)

### Design decisions (mine, session 3)

- Dedup before row 0, per the brief's "remove the duplicates before
  modelling". The "as printed" line is the analyst's own output, not
  re-computed; the harness check on the raw file confirms the wiring.
- "Building data" for rows 0–2 = the training window only (≤ 2025-06), so
  the test window is scored exactly once, at row 3. Row 0 therefore differs
  from "as printed" in two ways at once (dedup, window); footnoted.
- Order 1→2→3→4 for the structural reasons in the prose.
- `StratifiedGroupKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)` for change 2:
  same stratification and seed as the analyst, grouping added, so the row
  differs from row 1 in the grouping alone.
- Validation month unused in A2 (nothing chosen from data). No bootstrap CI
  on the segment AUCs: not asked for, page budget.
- No single-column reference on the test window: "score once" honoured.
- Model never touched: `analyst_pipeline()` imported unmodified.

### Arguing against the draft

- Row 4 corporate at 0.404: 34 churners. Rough SE of an AUC near 0.5 with
  34 positives and 826 negatives is about 0.05, so 0.40 is ~2 SE off, not
  pure noise. But 34 is 34. A3's corporate dollar line will be fragile
  whatever the AUC says.
- The pooled 0.644 hides the corporate number. A book at 35% corporate is
  not described by it. This is the A3 problem.
- Row 3 (0.644) is below A1's best single-column AUC (0.681), but those are
  different rows (all months vs test window). Not comparable as they stand;
  a test-window single-column reference would settle it but would score the
  test set a second time. Not done.
- `app_opens_last_30d` flips sign in the multivariable model (OR 1.12 per SD)
  versus its single-column direction in A1. Given sessions and minutes,
  opens without workouts may be a bad sign. Do not quote the single-column
  direction and the coefficient in the same breath.
- The order-independence example (3 before 1 leaves AUC near 0.97) is
  reasoned, not computed. Computing it would score the test set with the
  leaking columns in. Not done; the reasoning is the rubric item.
- Change 2 ≈ 0 in any order on this data is a coincidence of a linear model
  with no member-identifying columns, not a general rule.

### Numbers used and where they live

| Number | File |
|---|---|
| 0.967 as printed | `analyst_model_output.txt` |
| harness check 0.967 on raw | `run.log` |
| 0.968 / 0.748 / 0.747 / 0.644 / 0.404 / 0.641; rows and churners per row; 21,031 / 1,767; 4,556 / 408; 860 / 34; 3,696 / 374 | `a2_table.csv` |
| 3,648 members; 2,899 (79.5%) in 2+ folds; 613 single-row members | `a2_fold_overlap.csv` |
| channel ORs 4.3 / 4.1 / 4.1; elite 0.38; sessions 0.57 per SD, 0.88 per unit; minutes 0.61; price 1.38; login 1.33; tenure 0.85 | `a2_odds_ratios.csv` |
| 12 kept / 2 dropped / 3 ids | `a2_columns.csv` |
| corporate 19% of test rows (860/4,556), 8% of test churners (34/408) | `a2_table.csv`, arithmetic |
| 533 corporate rows in training window, tenure ≤ 6 | `a1_corporate_segment.csv` |
| 1,810 exit-survey rows, all churners | `a1_column_timing.csv` |
| test-window predictions for A3 | `a2_test_scores.csv` |

content.text:
Pulled and verified. Three things before the A3 design.

**Cross-machine reproducibility holds.** Re-running everything on the Mac leaves `a2_table.csv` and all six A1 outputs byte-identical to what Windows committed. Only `a2_test_scores.csv` moved, by at most **4×10⁻¹⁴** in `p_churn` — ARM vs x86 floating-point noise, identical to 10 decimal places. It matters for A3 that I checked the thing that could have bitten: **the same 203 rows** fall above the cost threshold on both machines, so the dollar figure will not depend on which laptop ran it. Worth a line in the process note.

**Schedule.** Due Thursday 1 Oct, 6:00 PM Central — two days. A3 is the last 20 points of Part A; Part B is 35 points and untouched, Handout 3 unread, and neither `memo.md` nor `ai_process_note.md` is started. That's your call to make, not mine, but it argues for keeping A3 tight today rather than exploring every option below.

## A3 design — your decisions

Item 1 is already done: test AUC overall 0.644 (4,556 rows, 408 churners), corporate 0.404 (860, 34), other 0.641 (3,696, 374), all from A2 row 3/4. Item 2 is arithmetic: offering is worth 66p − 18(1−p) = 84p − 18, which beats 0 when **p > 18/84 = 0.2143**. Neither needs a decision. These do:

**D1 — What counts as one offer.** The program scores the active book monthly, so a member present in all three test months can be offered three times. (a) Every qualifying member-month is an offer — matches the brief's per-offer economics and the monthly program. (b) At most one offer per member across the window. (c) (a) headline, (b) as a one-line sensitivity. *I'd take (a)*; it's the unit everything else in Part A uses.

**D2 — Reporting period.** The test window is exactly one quarter. (a) One figure for Oct–Dec — directly comparable to the analyst's $19,774/quarter. (b) Per month. (c) Quarter headline plus the monthly split. *I'd take (c)*: the monthly split is three numbers and shows whether the value is stable.

**D3 — What to price alongside it.** Required: t* versus offer-everyone. Optional additions: no program ($0, the do-nothing floor — R1 §1's "distance from something"); the analyst's 0.267 threshold; the full value-versus-threshold curve. The curve is the interesting one and the risky one: plotting it is *reporting*, not selecting, since t* was derived from the finance table before anything was scored — but it will look like test-set shopping unless the memo is explicit. *I'd take t\* + offer-everyone + $0, and add the analyst's 0.267 only if you want to make the "derived versus grid-searched" point numerically.*

**D4 — Calibration, and where.** The threshold multiplies p by money, so it assumes p is a real probability, not just a ranking (R1 §4.7). The validation month (Sep 2025) is still unused and is exactly the place for this — it is not the test set. (a) Check calibration on Sep 2025, report it as a caveat, leave t* as derived. (b) Check on the test window itself, reporting only. (c) Skip it. *I'd take (a).* It needs one addition to `a2_evaluation.py` — save validation-month scores alongside the test scores — so that A3 still never rescores the test set.

**D5 — Segment dollars.** Overall only, or overall plus corporate/other? Corporate ranks below a coin flip, so its dollar line may well be negative, and the book is forecast at 35% corporate. *I'd report both* — it's the evidence your recommendation's condition will rest on.

**D6 — The recommendation.** Yours entirely. The brief wants a condition someone at Northline could check: a share of the book, or a measured AUC. Worth deciding before you see the dollar figure, so the number doesn't write the verdict for you.

Three things I'll carry into the caveats whatever you choose: the test quarter is Oct–Dec (8.4–9.5% base rate) but deployment is Apr–Jun (5.3–7.1% in 2025), so there are fewer churners to find; `winback_offer_sent` is 1 on 1,294 non-churners, meaning part of the history is already post-treatment; and the analyst's $19,774 used a threshold grid-searched on leaked out-of-fold scores, so it isn't a like-for-like comparison.

The test window's 4,556 rows come from only **1,669 distinct members** — 1,376 of them appear in all three months. So the same person shows up repeatedly, and the question is whether an "offer" is a row or a person.

At the threshold, **203 rows** are above 0.2143, and those rows belong to **166 distinct members**: 132 flagged once, 31 flagged twice, 3 flagged in all three months.

So the decision is literally what you multiply by $18:

- **(a) One offer per member-month — 203 offers.** The program as the brief describes it "scores every active member at the start of each month" and sends the top scorers an offer. A member who still looks risky in November gets contacted again in November. This is the operating reality of a monthly program.
- **(b) One offer per member — 166 offers.** You'd refuse to re-contact someone you already gave a month at 50% off.

Two reasons I lean to (a) beyond it matching the program description. First, the brief's economics are defined per offer: $18 each, $66 if it lands on a would-be churner. Second — and this is the awkward part of (b) — the label lives on one specific row. A churner has exactly one flagged row, their final month. So a member flagged in October and November who cancels in December generates, under (a), two wasted offers at −$18 and one good offer at +$66. Under (b) you'd have to pick *which* of their three months the single offer happened in, and if you picked October you'd score it as a wasted offer on a member who did in fact churn. That's an artefact of the accounting, not a real business fact.

Where (b) earns its place is as a one-line sensitivity: 37 of the 203 offers are repeat contacts, so a "contact each member at most once per quarter" policy would cost $666 less in offers and forgo whatever those repeats caught. That's cheap to report and pre-empts the obvious question from the VP.

The related judgment, which is yours and which the memo should probably name: the $240 LTV is a *lifetime* value, so if an offer retains someone in October, counting a second $66 for retaining them again in December would be double-counting. Under (a) that can't happen — only one row per churner carries the label — but it's worth being able to say why.

for D4 - what is the calibration you are talking about. the number p is the prediction coming out of the last (4th) model from A2 correct? this would mean that we know exactly what units the p is?

Three separate things. Taking them in the order that matters least to most.

## D5 — not quite; the brief splits them

Re-reading A3: item 1 requires **AUC** overall, corporate, and everyone else, each with row and churner counts — that's mandatory, and the rubric repeats it ("Test AUC overall and by segment with row and churner counts"). Item 3 asks for "the realised dollar value of the program on the test period at that threshold, and compare it with offering to every member" — no segment requirement.

So segment dollars are *optional*. I still recommend them, because your recommendation's condition will almost certainly be about corporate, and "corporate loses $X" is a far stronger sentence than "corporate ranks at 0.404." But it's a choice, not an obligation, and it costs a couple of lines of your page budget.

## D6 — why the shape comes first

The exam-ready version is two sentences: **the evidence you already have tells you the direction; the dollar figure only tells you the magnitude.** And a recommendation that a single realised number could flip isn't a recommendation — it's a readout of that number.

Unpacking it, four reasons:

1. **The figure is one realisation, not the risk.** Same distinction we worked through in session 2: the realised value on 4,556 rows with 408 churners is an empirical quantity with sampling error, not the expected value of the programme. If its sign decides your verdict, your verdict inherits its noise.

2. **The direction is already determined by things the number can't change.** Honest AUC 0.644 against a claimed 0.967; corporate at 0.404, below chance; corporate going from 19% of the test book to a forecast 35%; the model's single largest term being the channel itself. Whether the quarter lands at +$8,000 or +$12,000, none of that moves.

3. **The condition has to come from a mechanism, not from a total.** "Deploy while corporate stays under X% of the book" is a claim about *why* the model earns money — it ranks non-corporate members and not corporate ones. You can only write that sentence from the structure. A dollar total can't tell you what to condition on.

4. **This is R1 §4.9's rule applied one level up.** "Choose the metric before fitting anything, and write it down. Choosing afterwards, from a table of several, is selection on the outcome — the same error as choosing a model on the test set."

And the reason that's worth doing rather than just principled: pre-committing is what makes you able to be **surprised**. Course doc §3 — "Write down what you expect before you compute anything... that is what makes you able to be surprised, and being surprised is how you find things." If you expect the corporate line to be negative and it comes out strongly positive, that's a finding worth chasing. If you had no expectation, it's just a number you write down. Deciding the shape first doesn't mean ignoring the number; it means the number can inform you instead of merely instructing you.

## D4 — what calibration is

First a correction: **p comes from the row-3 model**, not a fourth model. Row 4 fits nothing — it takes row 3's 4,556 scores and splits them by channel. There are only four fits in A2 (rows 0, 1, 2 inside folds; row 3 once on the training window).

Now the substance. You're right that p is unitless and that we *call* it a probability — the model outputs a number in (0,1) and we label it "probability this member-month ends in cancellation." Calibration is the question of whether that label is **true**: among all the rows where the model said p ≈ 0.25, did about 25% actually churn? (R1 §4.7: "A model is calibrated if, among accounts assigned p̂ ≈ 0.2, about 20% default.")

The reason this is a real question and not pedantry: **AUC cannot see it.** AUC is a statement about ordering only — R1 §4.5 spells it out, "a model whose probabilities are all ten times too large has exactly the same AUC." So our 0.644 tells us the model ranks tolerably and tells us *nothing* about whether p = 0.25 means 25%.

And it matters here specifically because of what we're about to do with p. The threshold derivation is 84p − 18 > 0, which treats p as a genuine probability. If the model is systematically over-confident — says 0.25 where the truth is 0.10 — then thresholding at 0.214 selects members whose real churn probability is well below 0.214, and every one of those offers loses money in expectation. The realised dollar figure would come out worse than the derivation promises, and without a calibration check we'd have no way to say why.

There's a concrete reason to suspect drift: the model was fitted where the base rate is **8.40%** (1,767 of 21,031) and applied where it is **8.96%** (408 of 4,556) — close, so probably fine here — but deployment is Apr–Jun, which ran 5.3–7.1% in 2025. """
A3 -- the targeting decision.  Northline Fitness churn.

Uses the final protocol from A2 and never rescores the test window: the
predictions come from `a2_test_scores.csv`, written by A2 row 3.

What happens here, in order, and the order matters:

    1. The cost-based threshold, derived from the finance table in the brief
       by taking the expectation at predicted probability p.  Two routes, both
       computed from the constants in starter/load.py rather than typed in.
    2. A calibration check on the validation month (2025-09).  The threshold
       multiplies p by money, so it assumes p is a probability and not merely
       a ranking (Handout R1 s4.7).  The validation month is the place the
       brief reserves for any choice made by looking at data; the test window
       is not touched.  Scoring the validation month needs the row-3 model, so
       it is refitted here through A2's own `fit_once` and `ADMISSIBLE` -- the
       same code path, deterministic, and A2 is left alone.
    3. Only then, the money: realised value on the test quarter at the derived
       threshold, against offering to everyone, against no programme, and at
       the threshold the analyst's script grid-searched.

The calibration verdict is set below, from the evidence in step 2, before any
dollar figure is computed.  Deciding it afterwards would be choosing the
correction by which version pays better.

Outputs, all in analysis/outputs/:
    a3_threshold.txt      the derivation, with the arithmetic printed
    a3_calibration.csv    reliability table on the validation month
    a3_value.csv          the A3 value exhibit: policies x segments
    a3_value_curve.csv    realised value across the threshold grid
    a3_value_curve.png    the same, as a figure
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ROOT = HERE.parents[1]
OUT = ROOT / "analysis" / "outputs"

sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))
from prep import (TARGET, TRAIN_END, VALID_MONTH, OFFER_COST, MEMBER_LTV,  # noqa: E402
                  OFFER_CONVERSION, load_clean, offer_value)
from a2_evaluation import ADMISSIBLE, fit_once  # noqa: E402

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Calibration decision.  Set from the validation-month check in step 2, on
# calibration evidence only, before any dollar figure was computed.
#   "raw"   -- predicted probabilities used as they come out of the model
#   "platt" -- corrected by a logistic fitted on the validation month
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
CALIBRATION = "raw"

N_CALIBRATION_BINS = 10
ANALYST_THRESHOLD = 0.267    # what analyst_model.py's grid search selected
CURVE_GRID = np.linspace(0.005, 0.6, 400)   # the analyst's grid, for the curve


def derive_threshold() -> tuple[float, list[str]]:
    """The cost-based threshold, derived rather than quoted.

    Everything comes from the constants in starter/load.py so the arithmetic
    cannot drift from the brief.
    """
    gain_churner = MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION - OFFER_COST   # offer lands on a churner
    cost_stayer = OFFER_COST                                    # offer lands on a stayer
    t = OFFER_COST / (MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION)
    # Same number by Handout R1 eq. (4), t* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN), with a
    # wasted offer as the false positive and a missed churner as the false
    # negative.  Two routes agreeing is the check.
    t_r1 = cost_stayer / (cost_stayer + gain_churner)
    assert abs(t - t_r1) < 1e-12, (t, t_r1)

    lines = [
        "Deriving the threshold from the finance table",
        "",
        f"  offer cost                     ${OFFER_COST:,.2f}",
        f"  lifetime value of a member     ${MEMBER_LTV:,.2f}",
        f"  fraction of churners retained  {OFFER_CONVERSION}",
        "",
        "An offer to a member who would have churned is worth",
        f"  {MEMBER_LTV:,.0f} x {OFFER_CONVERSION} - {OFFER_COST:,.0f} = ${gain_churner:,.2f}",
        "An offer to a member who would not have churned costs",
        f"  ${cost_stayer:,.2f}",
        "No offer is worth $0.",
        "",
        "At predicted probability p the expected value of offering is",
        f"  E[value | p] = p x {gain_churner:,.0f} + (1 - p) x (-{cost_stayer:,.0f})"
        f" = {gain_churner + cost_stayer:,.0f}p - {cost_stayer:,.0f}",
        "",
        "Offering beats not offering when that expectation exceeds 0:",
        f"  {gain_churner + cost_stayer:,.0f}p - {cost_stayer:,.0f} > 0",
        f"  p > {cost_stayer:,.0f} / {gain_churner + cost_stayer:,.0f}"
        f" = {OFFER_COST:,.0f} / ({MEMBER_LTV:,.0f} x {OFFER_CONVERSION})",
        f"  p > {t:.6f}",
        "",
        f"Threshold t* = {t:.4f}.  Offer to every member scored above it.",
        "",
        "Cross-check, Handout R1 eq. (4): t* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN) with a",
        f"wasted offer C_FP = ${cost_stayer:,.0f} and a missed churner",
        f"C_FN = ${gain_churner:,.0f} gives {cost_stayer:,.0f}/"
        f"({cost_stayer:,.0f}+{gain_churner:,.0f}) = {t_r1:.6f}.  Same number.",
        "",
        "Note this depends only on the finance figures, not on the data, and",
        "was fixed before any test-window score was read.  The analyst's",
        f"script instead grid-searched {ANALYST_THRESHOLD} by maximising realised value",
        "on its own out-of-fold predictions, which is a choice made by looking",
        "at outcomes.",
    ]
    return t, lines


def logit(p: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    return np.log(p / (1 - p))


def reliability(y: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, bins: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Equal-count bins: mean predicted probability against observed rate."""
    order = np.argsort(p)
    groups = np.array_split(order, bins)
    rows = []
    for i, idx in enumerate(groups, start=1):
        rows.append({
            "bin": i,
            "rows": len(idx),
            "mean_predicted": round(float(p[idx].mean()), 4),
            "observed_rate": round(float(y[idx].mean()), 4),
            "churners": int(y[idx].sum()),
        })
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["predicted_minus_observed"] = (out["mean_predicted"] - out["observed_rate"]).round(4)
    return out


def calibration_check(model) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, LogisticRegression, list[str]]:
    """Score the validation month and ask whether p means what it claims."""
    df, _ = load_clean()
    val = df[df["month"] == VALID_MONTH].reset_index(drop=True)
    y = val[TARGET].to_numpy()
    p = model.predict_proba(val[ADMISSIBLE])[:, 1]

    table = reliability(y, p, N_CALIBRATION_BINS)

    # Platt scaling: a logistic regression of the outcome on the log-odds of
    # the model's own score.  If the model were already calibrated the fit
    # would be slope 1, intercept 0, so the coefficients read directly as
    # "how far off, and in which direction".
    platt = LogisticRegression().fit(logit(p).reshape(-1, 1), y)
    slope = float(platt.coef_[0][0])
    intercept = float(platt.intercept_[0])

    lines = [
        f"Calibration check on the validation month ({VALID_MONTH})",
        f"  rows {len(val):,}   churners {int(y.sum()):,}   "
        f"observed rate {y.mean():.4f}",
        f"  mean predicted probability      {p.mean():.4f}",
        f"  observed minus predicted        {y.mean() - p.mean():+.4f}",
        f"  AUC on the validation month     {roc_auc_score(y, p):.4f}",
        f"  Platt slope {slope:.4f}, intercept {intercept:+.4f} "
        f"(1.0 and 0.0 would be perfectly calibrated)",
    ]
    return table, platt, lines


def apply_calibration(p: np.ndarray, platt: LogisticRegression) -> np.ndarray:
    if CALIBRATION == "raw":
        return p
    if CALIBRATION == "platt":
        return platt.predict_proba(logit(p).reshape(-1, 1))[:, 1]
    raise ValueError(CALIBRATION)


def value_of(y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """Realised dollars from a set of targeting decisions.

    Vectorised, then checked row by row against the supplied offer_value()
    helper so the economics come from the starter module, not from here.
    """
    v = np.where(offered, np.where(y == 1,
                                   MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION - OFFER_COST,
                                   -OFFER_COST), 0.0)
    check = np.array([offer_value(int(c), bool(o)) for c, o in zip(y, offered)])
    assert np.allclose(v, check), "vectorised value disagrees with offer_value()"
    return float(v.sum())


def main() -> None:
    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    # ---- 1. the threshold ----------------------------------------------------
    t_star, lines = derive_threshold()
    (OUT / "a3_threshold.txt").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print("\n".join(lines))
    print()

    # ---- 2. calibration, on the validation month -----------------------------
    df, _ = load_clean()
    build = df[df["month"] <= TRAIN_END].reset_index(drop=True)
    model = fit_once(build, ADMISSIBLE)          # the row-3 model, same code path
    table, platt, cal_lines = calibration_check(model)
    table.to_csv(OUT / "a3_calibration.csv", index=False)
    print("\n".join(cal_lines))
    print()
    print(table.to_string(index=False))
    print()
    print(f"calibration setting in use: {CALIBRATION}")
    print()

    # ---- 3. the money, on the test window that A2 already scored -------------
    scores = pd.read_csv(OUT / "a2_test_scores.csv")
    y = scores[TARGET].to_numpy()
    p = apply_calibration(scores["p_churn"].to_numpy(), platt)
    scores["p_used"] = p

    policies = {
        f"targeted at t* = {t_star:.4f}": p > t_star,
        "offer to every member-month": np.ones(len(scores), dtype=bool),
        "no programme": np.zeros(len(scores), dtype=bool),
        f"targeted at the analyst's {ANALYST_THRESHOLD}": p > ANALYST_THRESHOLD,
    }

    rows = []
    for name, offered in policies.items():
        for seg in ("all", "corporate", "other"):
            m = (np.ones(len(scores), dtype=bool) if seg == "all"
                 else scores["segment"].eq(seg).to_numpy())
            o = offered & m
            rows.append({
                "policy": name,
                "segment": seg,
                "rows_scored": int(m.sum()),
                "churners": int(y[m].sum()),
                "offers": int(o.sum()),
                "offers_to_churners": int((o & (y == 1)).sum()),
                "offers_wasted": int((o & (y == 0)).sum()),
                "value_usd": round(value_of(y[m], o[m]), 2),
            })
    value = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    value.to_csv(OUT / "a3_value.csv", index=False)

    # Sensitivity: the same policy, but a member is contacted at most once
    # across the quarter (the first month they clear the threshold).
    flagged = scores.loc[p > t_star].copy()
    first_only = flagged.sort_values(["member_id", "month"]).groupby("member_id").head(1)
    repeat_offers = len(flagged) - len(first_only)
    v_first = value_of(first_only[TARGET].to_numpy(),
                       np.ones(len(first_only), dtype=bool))

    # ---- the value curve: the same scores read at many cut points ------------
    curve = pd.DataFrame({
        "threshold": CURVE_GRID,
        "offers": [(p > t).sum() for t in CURVE_GRID],
        "value_usd": [round(value_of(y, p > t), 2) for t in CURVE_GRID],
    })
    curve.to_csv(OUT / "a3_value_curve.csv", index=False)

    import matplotlib
    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
    ax.plot(curve["threshold"], curve["value_usd"], "-", label="realised value")
    ax.axhline(0, lw=0.8, color="0.6")
    v_star = float(curve.loc[(curve["threshold"] - t_star).abs().idxmin(), "value_usd"])
    ax.axvline(t_star, ls="--", color="C1")
    ax.annotate(f"derived t* = {t_star:.3f}\n${v_star:,.0f}", (t_star, v_star),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(12, -28), fontsize=9, color="C1")
    ax.axvline(ANALYST_THRESHOLD, ls=":", color="C2")
    v_analyst = float(curve.loc[(curve["threshold"] - ANALYST_THRESHOLD).abs().idxmin(), "value_usd"])
    ax.annotate(f"analyst's {ANALYST_THRESHOLD}\n${v_analyst:,.0f}", (ANALYST_THRESHOLD, v_analyst),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(12, 16), fontsize=9, color="C2")
    ax.set_xlabel("threshold on predicted churn probability")
    ax.set_ylabel("realised value on the test quarter (USD)")
    ax.set_title("A3: realised value across thresholds, Oct-Dec 2025\n"
                 "threshold derived from the finance table before scoring; "
                 "the curve is shown for sensitivity, not for selection",
                 fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(OUT / "a3_value_curve.png", dpi=150)

    print("A3 value exhibit (test quarter, Oct-Dec 2025)")
    print(value.to_string(index=False))
    print()
    print(f"repeat-contact sensitivity: of {len(flagged)} offers at t*, "
          f"{repeat_offers} are repeat contacts of a member already offered "
          f"earlier in the quarter; contacting each member at most once gives "
          f"{len(first_only)} offers worth ${v_first:,.0f}")
    print()
    print(f"wrote {OUT / 'a3_threshold.txt'}, a3_calibration.csv, a3_value.csv, "
          f"a3_value_curve.csv, a3_value_curve.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

A3 -- the targeting decision.  Northline Fitness churn.

Uses the final protocol from A2 and never rescores the test window: the
predictions come from `a2_test_scores.csv`, written by A2 row 3.

What happens here, in order, and the order matters:

    1. The cost-based threshold, derived from the finance table in the brief
       by taking the expectation at predicted probability p.  Two routes, both
       computed from the constants in starter/load.py rather than typed in.
    2. A calibration check on the validation month (2025-09).  The threshold
       multiplies p by money, so it assumes p is a probability and not merely
       a ranking (Handout R1 s4.7).  The validation month is the place the
       brief reserves for any choice made by looking at data; the test window
       is not touched.  Scoring the validation month needs the row-3 model, so
       it is refitted here through A2's own `fit_once` and `ADMISSIBLE` -- the
       same code path, deterministic, and A2 is left alone.
    3. Only then, the money: realised value on the test quarter at the derived
       threshold, against offering to everyone, against no programme, and at
       the threshold the analyst's script grid-searched.

dollar figure is computed.  Deciding it afterwards would be choosing the
correction by which version pays better.

    a3_threshold.txt      the derivation, with the arithmetic printed
    a3_calibration.csv    reliability table on the validation month

    a3_value_curve.csv    realised value across the threshold grid

        f" = {OFFER_COST:,.0f} / ({MEMBER_LTV:,.0f} x {OFFER_CONVERSION})",

content.text:
Two things, one of which is a correction to what I told you earlier.

**Validation evidence (the basis for the decision):**

- Platt slope **0.788**, intercept **−0.219**. If the only problem were September being a high-churn month, the fix would be a level shift and the slope would come out near 1.0. It doesn't — the model's log-odds are too spread out, which is a property of the model, not of the month.
- Under-prediction in **8 of the 10 bins**, including the top bin where our threshold lives: predicted 0.265 against 0.290 observed.
- Validation AUC 0.695, so the ranking is fine. This is purely about the numbers attached to the ranking — exactly the split R1 §4.5 warns about.

**My earlier caution was wrong.** I said fitting on September (10.8% base rate) would over-correct upward for a test window nearer the training rate. The raw model's mean prediction on the test window is 0.0738, i.e. it under-predicts there too, because the test book is more corporate and the model assigns corporate low risk. So the correction moves in the right direction, not the wrong one.

**And a disclosure about how I found that out.** To check the direction I compared mean predicted against observed *on the test window*, and it came out raw 0.0738 versus corrected 0.0926 against an observed 0.0896. That is test-set information, and it must not be the reason we correct — using it that way would be selecting on the test set. The decision has to rest on the validation evidence above, which independently says correct: slope 0.788, systematic under-prediction through the decision region. The test comparison can be *reported* afterwards as a check that the correction did what validation predicted, the same way the test AUC is reported. I'd rather tell you I computed it than quietly not mention it.

**Mechanical effect:** 203 rows clear the threshold on raw scores, 242 on corrected. Both Platt and isotonic are monotone, so **the A2 AUCs are unchanged** — 0.644, 0.404, 0.641 all still describe the model producing the dollars.

So: set `CALIBRATION = "platt"`, on the validation evidence, and report the raw figure as a sensitivity line? Or stay raw and state the miscalibration as a caveat? I'd correct — the threshold derivation treats p as a probability and the validation month says it isn't one.
we should definitely calibrate since that is what the loss function is expecting, but can you explain what you mean by sensitivity line?

A "sensitivity" is one extra line showing what the answer would have been under a different assumption, so the reader can see how much the conclusion depends on that assumption rather than having to take it on faith. It's not a second answer — it's a measure of how load-bearing a choice was.

You've already agreed to one: the repeat-contact line. The headline counts 203 offers; the sensitivity says "37 of those are repeat contacts; at most one contact per member it's 166 offers worth $Z." If $Z is close to the headline, the choice didn't matter much and nobody needs to argue about it. If it's wildly different, the VP has learned that the programme's value hinges on re-contacting people.

The calibration one would be the same move: headline on corrected probabilities, one line saying "on uncorrected probabilities the figure would have been $W." Its job is to show whether correcting was a detail or the whole ballgame — and it pre-empts the obvious challenge, since a reader who distrusts the correction can see immediately whether it changes the recommendation.

Two reasons it's worth the line here, and one against. For: the correction is the one place in A3 where we fitted something to data, so it's the most attackable step; and it costs a single sentence. Against: your §1 budget is already 1,051 words of prose across A1 and A2 before A3 exists.

Given it's a sentence and it defends the step most likely to be questioned, I'd keep it. Setting `CALIBRATION = "platt"` and running.

Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.278/1a9b1ae4fe9c532b82209648b14295e1/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

LINE = "#20486b"      # the one series
MARK_T = "#c2570c"    # the derived threshold
MARK_A = "#4a7c2f"    # the analyst's threshold
INK = "#1a1a1a"       # label text: ink, never the series colour
MUTED = "#6b6b6b"


def value_curve_figure(curve: pd.DataFrame, t_star: float) -> None:
    """Realised value against the decision threshold, in two panels.

    One panel cannot carry this: offering to (almost) everyone loses tens of
    thousands, so on a single axis the region that decides the programme is a
    flat line on the zero gridline.  Left panel is the full range, right panel
    the decision region at its own scale.  Same series, same units, two views.
    """
    import matplotlib
    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    def at(t):
        return float(curve.loc[(curve["threshold"] - t).abs().idxmin(), "value_usd"])

    v_star, v_analyst = at(t_star), at(ANALYST_THRESHOLD)
    peak = curve.loc[curve["value_usd"].idxmax()]

    fig, (ax_full, ax_zoom) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.3))

    for ax in (ax_full, ax_zoom):
        ax.axhline(0, lw=0.9, color=MUTED, zorder=1)
        ax.plot(curve["threshold"], curve["value_usd"], "-", lw=2,
                color=LINE, zorder=3)
        ax.axvline(t_star, ls="--", lw=1.4, color=MARK_T, zorder=2)
        ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
        ax.spines[["left", "bottom"]].set_color(MUTED)
        ax.tick_params(colors=MUTED, labelsize=9)
        ax.set_xlabel("threshold on predicted churn probability",
                      fontsize=9, color=INK)

    # ---- left: the whole range, so the cost of blanket offers is visible ----
    ax_full.set_ylabel("realised value, Oct-Dec 2025 (USD)", fontsize=9, color=INK)
    ax_full.set_title("Full range", fontsize=10, color=INK, loc="left")
    ax_full.annotate(f"offer to everyone\n${curve['value_usd'].iloc[0]:,.0f}",
                     (curve["threshold"].iloc[0], curve["value_usd"].iloc[0]),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(14, 6),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
    ax_full.annotate(f"t* = {t_star:.3f}", (t_star, 0),
                     textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, -34),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
    ax_full.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((0.15, -3000), 0.30, 5000, fill=False,
                                    ec=MUTED, lw=0.8, ls=":", zorder=4))
    ax_full.annotate("detail, right", (0.45, 2000), textcoords="offset points",
                     xytext=(-6, 10), fontsize=8, color=MUTED, ha="right")

    # ---- right: the decision region at a scale that can be read ------------
    ax_zoom.axvline(ANALYST_THRESHOLD, ls=":", lw=1.4, color=MARK_A, zorder=2)
    ax_zoom.set_xlim(0.15, 0.45)
    ax_zoom.set_ylim(-3000, 2000)
    ax_zoom.set_title("Decision region (detail)", fontsize=10, color=INK, loc="left")
    ax_zoom.plot([t_star], [v_star], "o", ms=8, color=MARK_T,
                 mec="white", mew=1.6, zorder=5)
    ax_zoom.annotate(f"derived t* = {t_star:.3f}\n${v_star:,.0f}", (t_star, v_star),

1	"""
2	A3 -- the targeting decision.  Northline Fitness churn.
3	
4	Uses the final protocol from A2 and never rescores the test window: the
5	predictions come from `a2_test_scores.csv`, written by A2 row 3.
6	
7	What happens here, in order, and the order matters:
8	
9	    1. The cost-based threshold, derived from the finance table in the brief
10	       by taking the expectation at predicted probability p.  Two routes, both
11	       computed from the constants in starter/load.py rather than typed in.
12	    2. A calibration check on the validation month (2025-09).  The threshold
13	       multiplies p by money, so it assumes p is a probability and not merely
14	       a ranking (Handout R1 s4.7).  The validation month is the place the
15	       brief reserves for any choice made by looking at data; the test window
16	       is not touched.  Scoring the validation month needs the row-3 model, so
17	       it is refitted here through A2's own `fit_once` and `ADMISSIBLE` -- the
18	       same code path, deterministic, and A2 is left alone.
19	    3. Only then, the money: realised value on the test quarter at the derived
20	       threshold, against offering to everyone, against no programme, and at
21	       the threshold the analyst's script grid-searched.
22	
23	The calibration verdict is set below, from the evidence in step 2, before any
24	dollar figure is computed.  Deciding it afterwards would be choosing the
25	correction by which version pays better.
26	
27	Outputs, all in analysis/outputs/:
28	    a3_threshold.txt      the derivation, with the arithmetic printed
29	    a3_calibration.csv    reliability table on the validation month
30	    a3_value.csv          the A3 value exhibit: policies x segments
31	    a3_value_curve.csv    realised value across the threshold grid
32	    a3_value_curve.png    the same, as a figure
33	"""
34	import sys
35	from pathlib import Path
36	
37	import numpy as np
38	import pandas as pd
39	from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
40	from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
41	
42	HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
43	ROOT = HERE.parents[1]
44	OUT = ROOT / "analysis" / "outputs"
45	
46	sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))
47	from prep import (TARGET, TRAIN_END, VALID_MONTH, OFFER_COST, MEMBER_LTV,  # noqa: E402
48	                  OFFER_CONVERSION, load_clean, offer_value)
49	from a2_evaluation import ADMISSIBLE, fit_once  # noqa: E402
50	
51	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
52	# Calibration decision.  Set from the validation-month check in step 2, on
53	# calibration evidence only, before any dollar figure was computed.
54	#   "raw"   -- predicted probabilities used as they come out of the model
55	#   "platt" -- corrected by a logistic fitted on the validation month
56	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
57	# Verdict from step 2, on validation evidence only: Platt slope 0.79 (1.0 would
58	# be calibrated) and under-prediction in 8 of 10 bins including the decision
59	# region.  A pure level shift from September being a high-churn month would
60	# have left the slope near 1.0; it did not, so the miscalibration is a
61	# property of the model.  Correct.
62	CALIBRATION = "platt"
63	
64	N_CALIBRATION_BINS = 10
65	ANALYST_THRESHOLD = 0.267    # what analyst_model.py's grid search selected
66	CURVE_GRID = np.linspace(0.005, 0.6, 400)   # the analyst's grid, for the curve
67	
68	
69	def derive_threshold() -> tuple[float, list[str]]:
70	    """The cost-based threshold, derived rather than quoted.
71	
72	    Everything comes from the constants in starter/load.py so the arithmetic
73	    cannot drift from the brief.
74	    """
75	    gain_churner = MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION - OFFER_COST   # offer lands on a churner
76	    cost_stayer = OFFER_COST                                    # offer lands on a stayer
77	    t = OFFER_COST / (MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION)
78	    # Same number by Handout R1 eq. (4), t* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN), with a
79	    # wasted offer as the false positive and a missed churner as the false
80	    # negative.  Two routes agreeing is the check.
81	    t_r1 = cost_stayer / (cost_stayer + gain_churner)
82	    assert abs(t - t_r1) < 1e-12, (t, t_r1)
83	
84	    lines = [
85	        "Deriving the threshold from the finance table",
86	        "",
87	        f"  offer cost                     ${OFFER_COST:,.2f}",
88	        f"  lifetime value of a member     ${MEMBER_LTV:,.2f}",
89	        f"  fraction of churners retained  {OFFER_CONVERSION}",
90	        "",
91	        "An offer to a member who would have churned is worth",
92	        f"  {MEMBER_LTV:,.0f} x {OFFER_CONVERSION} - {OFFER_COST:,.0f} = ${gain_churner:,.2f}",
93	        "An offer to a member who would not have churned costs",
94	        f"  ${cost_stayer:,.2f}",
95	        "No offer is worth $0.",
96	        "",
97	        "At predicted probability p the expected value of offering is",
98	        f"  E[value | p] = p x {gain_churner:,.0f} + (1 - p) x (-{cost_stayer:,.0f})"
99	        f" = {gain_churner + cost_stayer:,.0f}p - {cost_stayer:,.0f}",
100	        "",
101	        "Offering beats not offering when that expectation exceeds 0:",
102	        f"  {gain_churner + cost_stayer:,.0f}p - {cost_stayer:,.0f} > 0",
103	        f"  p > {cost_stayer:,.0f} / {gain_churner + cost_stayer:,.0f}"
104	        f" = {OFFER_COST:,.0f} / ({MEMBER_LTV:,.0f} x {OFFER_CONVERSION})",
105	        f"  p > {t:.6f}",
106	        "",
107	        f"Threshold t* = {t:.4f}.  Offer to every member scored above it.",
108	        "",
109	        "Cross-check, Handout R1 eq. (4): t* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN) with a",
110	        f"wasted offer C_FP = ${cost_stayer:,.0f} and a missed churner",
111	        f"C_FN = ${gain_churner:,.0f} gives {cost_stayer:,.0f}/"
112	        f"({cost_stayer:,.0f}+{gain_churner:,.0f}) = {t_r1:.6f}.  Same number.",
113	        "",
114	        "Note this depends only on the finance figures, not on the data, and",
115	        "was fixed before any test-window score was read.  The analyst's",
116	        f"script instead grid-searched {ANALYST_THRESHOLD} by maximising realised value",
117	        "on its own out-of-fold predictions, which is a choice made by looking",
118	        "at outcomes.",
119	    ]
120	    return t, lines
121	
122	
123	def logit(p: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
124	    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
125	    return np.log(p / (1 - p))
126	
127	
128	def reliability(y: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, bins: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
129	    """Equal-count bins: mean predicted probability against observed rate."""
130	    order = np.argsort(p)
131	    groups = np.array_split(order, bins)
132	    rows = []
133	    for i, idx in enumerate(groups, start=1):
134	        rows.append({
135	            "bin": i,
136	            "rows": len(idx),
137	            "mean_predicted": round(float(p[idx].mean()), 4),
138	            "observed_rate": round(float(y[idx].mean()), 4),
139	            "churners": int(y[idx].sum()),
140	        })
141	    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
142	    out["predicted_minus_observed"] = (out["mean_predicted"] - out["observed_rate"]).round(4)
143	    return out
144	
145	
146	def calibration_check(model) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, LogisticRegression, list[str]]:
147	    """Score the validation month and ask whether p means what it claims."""
148	    df, _ = load_clean()
149	    val = df[df["month"] == VALID_MONTH].reset_index(drop=True)
150	    y = val[TARGET].to_numpy()
151	    p = model.predict_proba(val[ADMISSIBLE])[:, 1]
152	
153	    table = reliability(y, p, N_CALIBRATION_BINS)
154	
155	    # Platt scaling: a logistic regression of the outcome on the log-odds of
156	    # the model's own score.  If the model were already calibrated the fit
157	    # would be slope 1, intercept 0, so the coefficients read directly as
158	    # "how far off, and in which direction".
159	    platt = LogisticRegression().fit(logit(p).reshape(-1, 1), y)
160	    slope = float(platt.coef_[0][0])

content.text:
Full run is clean — 11.6 seconds, A3 included. Here are the numbers.

## Exhibit A3 — realised value, test quarter (Oct–Dec 2025)

| Policy | Offers | To churners | Wasted | Value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Targeted at t\* = 0.2143** | 242 | 62 | 180 | **+$852** |
| Offer to every member-month | 4,556 | 408 | 4,148 | **−$47,736** |
| No programme | 0 | — | — | $0 |
| At the analyst's 0.267 | 108 | 33 | 75 | +$828 |

Threshold derivation: an offer to a churner is worth 240 × 0.35 − 18 = $66, to a stayer −$18, so E[value | p] = 84p − 18, positive when **p > 18/84 = 0.2143**. Cross-checks against R1 eq. (4), 18/(18+66), to the same number — both routes are computed from the starter constants in `a3_threshold.txt`.

By segment: **corporate −$78** (9 offers, 1 churner), **everyone else +$930** (233 offers, 61 churners).

## The thing I want to flag: $852 is a very small number

Not too good — too *small*, and that's the finding. Against the analyst's claimed $19,774/quarter it's a **23× overstatement**, but in absolute terms the honest programme earns about **$3.52 per offer on $18 spent**, roughly a 20% return on offer spend, and **~$3,400/year** on a book of 1,669 members — for a programme that requires monthly scoring and 242 personal check-ins a quarter.

The arithmetic behind why is worth having in the memo, because it's the real business constraint: the offer economics demand **precision above 21.4%** to break even, and the base rate is **9%**. You need a 2.4× lift just to stop losing money. The model achieves 25.6% precision in the top 5.3% of the book — barely clear. Corporate achieves **11.1%**, well below break-even, which is why its line is negative.

Two things that make $852 likely optimistic for the actual deployment window: April–June ran 5.3–7.1% churn against the test quarter's 9.0%, so fewer members clear a fixed threshold and there are fewer churners to find; and the book is forecast to go from 19% corporate to 35%, shifting weight onto the segment that loses money.

## Secondary findings, two of which change what the memo should say

- **The threshold was not the analyst's main error.** Their grid-searched 0.267 yields $828 against our derived $852 — a $24 difference. Deriving the threshold is right and the brief requires it, but the memo shouldn't imply it's where the money is. The gap from $19,774 to $852 is the leaked columns and the evaluation design, not the cut point.
- **Calibration cost us $30.** Raw scores would have given $882; corrected give $852. Worth noting precisely because it demonstrates the discipline — we chose the correction on validation evidence before computing any dollars, and it made the headline slightly worse. Had we chosen on dollars we'd have kept the raw scores.
- **Not selecting on the test set cost $264.** The curve peaks at $1,098 at threshold 0.236; we took $852 at the derived 0.214. Honest to report, and it's what the right-hand panel of the figure shows.
- Repeat contacts: 47 of the 242 offers, worth $78 between them; one-contact-per-member gives 195 offers worth $774.

## Where this leaves your recommendation

Shape 4 + 5 still fits, and the numbers sharpen it: excluding corporate moves the quarter from $852 to $930, and corporate's 11.1% precision against a 21.4% break-even is the mechanism to cite. But the tripwire now has a harder job than "is the AUC holding up" — at $3.52 per offer the programme is close enough to break-even that a modest drop in precision, or the April base rate being lower than October's, would put it underwater. Whether that's worth running at all is your call, and it's a legitimate fourth option alongside the three we discussed.

Yes — and it's sharper than hypothetical. Two of our three test months are already at or below break-even.

| Month | Base rate | Offers | Precision | Value | Per offer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Oct 2025 | 9.5% | 114 | 21.9% | +$48 | $0.42 |
| Nov 2025 | 8.9% | 81 | 33.3% | +$810 | $10.00 |
| Dec 2025 | 8.4% | 47 | 21.3% | −$6 | −$0.13 |
| **Quarter** | 9.0% | 242 | 25.6% | **+$852** | $3.52 |

The whole $852 is essentially November. But the right reading isn't "December is a bad month" — with 47 offers, December's precision carries a standard error of about 6 points, so it's noise. The right reading is that **the programme sits close enough to break-even that ordinary month-to-month variation straddles zero.**

## The mechanism is calibration, not the base rate

This matters for where you point the tripwire. Value per offer is exactly 84 × (precision − 0.2143). If the model were perfectly calibrated, a fixed threshold would be **self-regulating**: you'd only ever offer to members whose true churn probability exceeds 21.4%, so every offer is positive in expectation no matter what the base rate is — a lower-churn April would simply produce *fewer* offers, not *worse* ones. Total value would shrink; value per offer would not go negative.

The danger is the model being wrong about p at the top of the range. Inside the offered set it predicts **28.6%** against an observed **25.6%** — it over-states the risk of exactly the members it selects, even after the Platt correction. That's what eats the margin. And an April book running 5.3–7.1% against a model fitted at 8.4% would push that over-prediction further in the same direction.

So the tripwire in your shape-5 should watch **realised precision in the offered set** (equivalently, realised value per offer), not only AUC. Two different things, and your instinct is right about one of them.

## The over-prediction is not about repeat contacts

It's what happens when you select the extreme tail of a noisy estimate. Within the 242 offered rows, split into quartiles by score:

| Quartile of offered set | Offers | Model says | Actually churned | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (just above t\*) | 61 | 22.2% | 18.0% | +4.1 |
| 2 | 60 | 24.3% | 23.3% | +0.9 |
| 3 | 60 | 28.1% | 33.3% | −5.2 |
| 4 (highest scores) | 61 | **39.6%** | **27.9%** | **+11.8** |

The worst over-statement is at the very top — the model's most confident predictions are its least reliable. That's the winner's curse: a member reaches the top of the ranking partly through genuine risk and partly through estimation error in their score, and the error doesn't repeat. Nothing to do with how often you contact them; it would happen on a single month's scoring of people you'd never contacted before.

With ~15 churners per quartile only the Q4 gap is much beyond noise (roughly 2 standard errors), so treat the row-by-row pattern as suggestive. The robust claim is the top-end one.

## But your instinct is separately correct

Repeat contacts *are* thinner:

| | Offers | Precision | Per offer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| First contact | 195 | 26.2% | **$3.97** |
| Repeat contacts | 47 | 23.4% | **$1.66** |

Both still clear the 21.4% break-even, so repeats aren't loss-making in aggregate — but they earn less than half as much per dollar spent. And the concrete version: **43 members were flagged more than once; 32 of them never churned in the window, and the programme spent $1,224 chasing them.**

So re-contacting is a real drag, just a second-order one next to the top-end over-confidence.

## What this settles

Your tripwire call is the right one and now has a specific form: **realised value per offer**, measured on matured 60-day outcomes, with $0 as the trip point — which is the same thing as realised precision falling below 21.4%. That single number catches both failure modes at once: it moves if the ranking degrades, and it moves if calibration drifts while the ranking holds.

Given the clock, I'd stop investigating here. Everything above already supports your recommendation shape, and none of it is required by the rubric. Shall I add the three things that *are* memo-bound to the script — monthly split, the ±$570 standard error, and first-versus-repeat per-offer value — then draft A3?

def per_offer_values(y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The realised dollars from each offer actually made, one per offer."""
    return np.where(y[offered] == 1,
                    MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION - OFFER_COST, -OFFER_COST)


def value_with_se(y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Total realised value and its standard error.

    Each offer returns +$66 or -$18, so the quarter's total is a sum of n
    such draws and its standard error is sd x sqrt(n).  Reported because the
    total sits close enough to zero that its uncertainty changes how it reads.
    """
    v = per_offer_values(y, offered)
    return float(v.sum()), float(v.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(len(v)))


def value_by_month(scores: pd.DataFrame, y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray,
                   t_star: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The same fixed threshold, month by month.

    Value per offer is exactly 84 x (precision - t*), so a month's programme
    is profitable precisely when the share of its offers that land on a
    churner exceeds the break-even precision, which is t* itself.
    """
    rows = []
    for month, idx in scores.groupby("month").groups.items():
        m = np.zeros(len(scores), dtype=bool)
        m[scores.index.get_indexer(idx)] = True
        o = offered & m
        n = int(o.sum())
        k = int((o & (y == 1)).sum())
        total, se = value_with_se(y, o) if n else (0.0, 0.0)
        rows.append({
            "month": month,
            "rows": int(m.sum()),
            "base_rate": round(float(y[m].mean()), 4),
            "offers": n,
            "offers_to_churners": k,
            "precision": round(k / n, 4) if n else np.nan,
            "break_even_precision": round(t_star, 4),
            "value_usd": round(total, 2),
            "value_se_usd": round(se, 2),
            "value_per_offer_usd": round(total / n, 2) if n else np.nan,
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def offer_quality(scores: pd.DataFrame, y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray,
                  t_star: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Where inside the offered set the value comes from, two cuts.

    First-versus-repeat contact is a property of the policy: a member may
    clear the threshold in more than one month.  The score quartiles are a
    property of the model: selecting the top of a noisy score means the
    highest scores are the most over-stated, so the gap between what the
    model claims and what it delivers is widest at the top.

    f = scores.loc[offered].copy()

    rows = []

    def add(cut, label, g):

        rows.append({

            "precision": round(prec, 4),
            "mean_predicted": round(float(g["p_used"].mean()), 4),
            "predicted_minus_observed": round(float(g["p_used"].mean()) - prec, 4),
            "value_usd": round(84.0 * n * (prec - t_star), 2),

def per_offer_values(y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """The realised dollars from each offer actually made, one per offer."""
    return np.where(y[offered] == 1,
                    MEMBER_LTV * OFFER_CONVERSION - OFFER_COST, -OFFER_COST)


def value_with_se(y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Total realised value and its standard error.

    Each offer returns +$66 or -$18, so the quarter's total is a sum of n
    such draws and its standard error is sd x sqrt(n).  Reported because the
    total sits close enough to zero that its uncertainty changes how it reads.
    """
    v = per_offer_values(y, offered)
    return float(v.sum()), float(v.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(len(v)))


def value_by_month(scores: pd.DataFrame, y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray,
                   t_star: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The same fixed threshold, month by month.

    Value per offer is exactly 84 x (precision - t*), so a month's programme
    is profitable precisely when the share of its offers that land on a
    churner exceeds the break-even precision, which is t* itself.
    """
    rows = []
    for month, idx in scores.groupby("month").groups.items():
        m = np.zeros(len(scores), dtype=bool)
        m[scores.index.get_indexer(idx)] = True
        o = offered & m
        n = int(o.sum())
        k = int((o & (y == 1)).sum())
        total, se = value_with_se(y, o) if n else (0.0, 0.0)
        rows.append({
            "month": month,
            "rows": int(m.sum()),
            "base_rate": round(float(y[m].mean()), 4),
            "offers": n,
            "offers_to_churners": k,
            "precision": round(k / n, 4) if n else np.nan,
            "break_even_precision": round(t_star, 4),
            "value_usd": round(total, 2),
            "value_se_usd": round(se, 2),
            "value_per_offer_usd": round(total / n, 2) if n else np.nan,
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def offer_quality(scores: pd.DataFrame, y: np.ndarray, offered: np.ndarray,
                  t_star: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Where inside the offered set the value comes from, two cuts.

    First-versus-repeat contact is a property of the policy: a member may
    clear the threshold in more than one month.  The score quartiles are a
    property of the model: selecting the top of a noisy score means the
    highest scores are the most over-stated, so the gap between what the
    model claims and what it delivers is widest at the top.
    """
    f = scores.loc[offered].copy()
    f["y"] = y[offered]
    f = f.sort_values(["member_id", "month"])
    f["contact_no"] = f.groupby("member_id").cumcount() + 1

    rows = []

    def add(cut, label, g):
        n, k = len(g), int(g["y"].sum())
        prec = k / n if n else np.nan
        rows.append({
            "cut": cut, "group": label, "offers": n, "offers_to_churners": k,
            "precision": round(prec, 4),
            "mean_predicted": round(float(g["p_used"].mean()), 4),
            "predicted_minus_observed": round(float(g["p_used"].mean()) - prec, 4),
            "value_usd": round(84.0 * n * (prec - t_star), 2),
            "value_per_offer_usd": round(84.0 * (prec - t_star), 2),
        })

    add("contact", "first contact", f[f["contact_no"] == 1])
    add("contact", "repeat contact", f[f["contact_no"] > 1])
    f["quartile"] = pd.qcut(f["p_used"], 4, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4])
    for q, g in f.groupby("quartile", observed=True):
        add("score quartile", f"Q{q} ({'lowest' if q == 1 else 'highest' if q == 4 else 'mid'})", g)
    add("all", "all offers", f)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

5	predictions come from `a2_test_scores.csv`, written by A2 row 3.
6

10	       by taking the expectation at predicted probability p.  Two routes, both
11	       computed from the constants in starter/load.py rather than typed in.
12	    2. A calibration check on the validation month (2025-09).  The threshold
13	       multiplies p by money, so it assumes p is a probability and not merely
14	       a ranking (Handout R1 s4.7).  The validation month is the place the
15	       brief reserves for any choice made by looking at data; the test window
16	       is not touched.  Scoring the validation month needs the row-3 model, so

19	    3. Only then, the money: realised value on the test quarter at the derived

21	       the threshold the analyst's script grid-searched.

25	correction by which version pays better.
