# A3 draft — the targeting decision

Draft for the A3 part of memo §1 (to the VP of Membership). Every number is in
`analysis/outputs/` from `bash analysis/run.sh` (session 4, 2026-09-29).

**Prose budget warning.** A1 is 499 words and A2 552, so §1 is at 1,051 before
this section. Two pages of prose is roughly 1,000–1,200 words. A3 below is
~430. Something has to come out — candidates at the end of this file.

---

## The recommendation (this leads memo §1)

> **Run the programme on non-corporate members only, and instrument it so it
> can be stopped.** On the test quarter it would have returned **$852**, not
> the $19,774 per quarter in the current proposal. Excluding corporate
> members raises that to **$930**: corporate offers landed on a churner 11% of
> the time against the 21.4% needed to break even, and corporate is forecast
> to grow from 19% of the book to 35%. Bring corporate back in only when it
> has enough history to be fitted on — today the training window holds 533
> corporate rows, none older than six months. Measure **realised value per
> offer** on matured 60-day outcomes each quarter and suspend the programme
> if it falls below zero, which is the same as the share of offers reaching a
> churner falling below 21.4%.

---

## Exhibit A3a — Test-window ranking, overall and by segment

Source: `analysis/outputs/a2_table.csv`. Fit on Jan 2024 – Jun 2025, scored
once on Oct – Dec 2025.

| Segment | Rows scored | Churners | AUC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| All | 4,556 | 408 | **0.644** |
| Corporate | 860 | 34 | **0.404** |
| Everyone else | 3,696 | 374 | **0.641** |

## Exhibit A3b — The threshold, derived from the finance table

Full working in `analysis/outputs/a3_threshold.txt`, computed from the
constants in `starter/load.py`.

An offer to a member who would have churned is worth 240 × 0.35 − 18 = **$66**.
An offer to a member who would not have churned costs **$18**. No offer is
worth $0. At predicted probability *p*,

  E[value of offering | p] = 66p − 18(1 − p) = **84p − 18**

which exceeds the $0 of not offering when

  **p > 18 / 84 = 0.2143**

Cross-check against the general form, t\* = C_FP / (C_FP + C_FN) with a wasted
offer at $18 and a missed churner at $66: 18/(18+66) = 0.2143. Same number.

Two things follow. The threshold depends only on the finance figures, not on
the data, and it was fixed before any test-window score was read. And 0.2143
is also the **break-even precision**: value per offer is exactly
84 × (precision − 0.2143), so the programme pays only while more than 21.4% of
its offers reach a member who would have cancelled.

## Exhibit A3c — Realised value on the test quarter

Source: `analysis/outputs/a3_value.csv`. Oct – Dec 2025, 4,556 member-months,
408 churners. One offer = one member-month.

| Policy | Offers | Reached a churner | Wasted | Value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **Targeted at t\* = 0.2143** | 242 | 62 | 180 | **+$852** |
| — corporate | 9 | 1 | 8 | **−$78** |
| — everyone else | 233 | 61 | 172 | **+$930** |
| Offer to every member-month | 4,556 | 408 | 4,148 | **−$47,736** |
| No programme | 0 | — | — | $0 |
| *Memo: at the analyst's 0.267* | 108 | 33 | 75 | +$828 |

The quarter's total carries a standard error of **$572** — each offer returns
+$66 or −$18, and the total is a sum of 242 such draws, so $852 sits 1.5
standard errors above zero.

## Exhibit A3d — Where the value comes from, and where it does not

Source: `analysis/outputs/a3_by_month.csv`, `a3_offer_quality.csv`.

| Month | Offers | Precision | Value | Per offer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Oct 2025 | 114 | 21.9% | +$48 | $0.42 |
| Nov 2025 | 81 | 33.3% | +$810 | $10.00 |
| Dec 2025 | 47 | 21.3% | −$6 | −$0.13 |

| Inside the offered set | Offers | Model says | Actually churned | Per offer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| First contact | 195 | 28.6% | 26.2% | $3.97 |
| Repeat contact | 47 | 28.4% | 23.4% | $1.66 |
| Q1, just above t\* | 61 | 22.2% | 18.0% | −$2.85 |
| Q4, highest scores | 61 | **39.6%** | **27.9%** | $5.41 |

**Figure A3** (`a3_value_curve.png`): realised value across the whole
threshold range, with the decision region at its own scale.

---

## Prose (draft, ~430 words; the recommendation above is the opening paragraph)

**What the programme is worth.** Using the protocol in Exhibit A2 — admissible
columns only, fitted on Jan 2024 to Jun 2025, scored once on Oct to Dec 2025 —
the targeting rule returns $852 on the quarter. The proposal in front of the
committee says $19,774. The gap is not the threshold: applying the analyst's
own 0.267 to honest scores returns $828, within $24 of our derived figure. The
gap is that their number was computed on predictions that had already seen the
cancellation, and on a random shuffle of two years rather than a fit to the
past scored on the future.

**Why the margin is thin.** An offer costs $18 and a retained churner returns
$66, so the programme pays only while more than 21.4% of offers reach someone
who would have cancelled. The base rate is 9%. That requires finding members at
roughly two and a half times the average risk, and the model manages 25.6% in
the top 5% of the book — profitable, but by four percentage points. Month to
month that margin straddles zero: November returned $810, October $48 and
December −$6. With 47 to 114 offers in a month those differences are mostly
noise, and that is the point — the programme sits close enough to break-even
that ordinary variation puts individual months on either side.

**Why corporate comes out.** Corporate members were ranked below a coin flip
(AUC 0.404 on 34 churners) and their nine offers landed on a churner once.
The model's single largest term is the acquisition channel itself, about four
times the churn odds for any non-corporate channel, learned from 533 corporate
rows none older than six months. It has learned that corporate members rarely
cancel, not which of them will. Excluding them adds $78 to the quarter and
removes a segment forecast to triple its share of the book.

**What to watch.** The threshold assumes the predicted probabilities mean what
they say. They roughly do — checked on the validation month, and corrected
there before use — but the model still overstates the risk of the members it
picks, claiming 39.6% for its top-scoring offers and delivering 27.9%. That is
what selecting the top of a noisy score does, and it is why the tripwire
should be a dollar figure rather than a ranking statistic: AUC can hold steady
while the probabilities drift and the cut point stops meaning what it meant.
Two further reasons to expect less than $852 next spring: April to June ran
5.3–7.1% churn against this quarter's 9.0%, and 1,294 members in the history
already received a retention contact, so part of the outcome we are fitting to
is itself post-treatment.

---

## Notes to self (not memo text)

### Design decisions (mine, session 4)

- One offer = one member-month, matching the monthly programme and the brief's
  per-offer economics. Per-member accounting was rejected: a churner has only
  one flagged row, so "which month did the single offer happen in" has no
  honest answer.
- Quarter as the reporting period (the test window is exactly one quarter).
  Monthly split added later, after it turned out to be informative rather than
  decorative — see below.
- Priced against offer-everyone, no programme, and the analyst's threshold.
  Declined to score the test window with the analyst's *model*: that would be
  a second scoring, and A2 already set the norm against it.
- Calibration checked on the validation month and corrected there. The verdict
  was set from validation evidence (Platt slope 0.79, under-prediction in 8 of
  10 bins) **before** any dollar figure existed. It cost $30 — raw scores give
  $882 — which is the point: chosen on calibration grounds, not on payout.
- Value curve reported. It re-reads the same scores at 400 cut points; no new
  scoring, and t* was fixed in advance. The curve peaks at $1,098 at 0.236;
  not selecting on the test set cost $264, stated in the memo rather than hidden.
- Recommendation shape chosen before the dollar figure was computed.

### Arguing against the draft

- **$852 ± $572 is 1.5 SE from zero.** A "deploy" that rests on it is resting
  on a coin that landed the right way. The scoped-and-instrumented shape is
  what the uncertainty supports; an unconditional go is not.
- **Corporate's −$78 is nine offers and one churner.** The dollar line is
  nearly meaningless on its own. The argument for exclusion rests on 34
  churners at AUC 0.404, 533 training rows, and the mechanism (the model learned
  the channel, not the members) — not on the $78.
- **The quartile table is suggestive, not conclusive.** ~15 churners per
  quartile; only the Q4 gap (39.6% claimed, 27.9% delivered) is about two
  standard errors. Do not present Q1–Q3 as an established pattern.
- **Repeat contacts are a second-order drag, not a defect.** $1.66 versus
  $3.97 per offer, both above break-even. Worth a sentence, not a policy fight.
  32 members were flagged more than once and never churned, costing $1,224.
- **Seasonality cuts both ways.** Oct–Dec is a *higher*-churn quarter than
  Apr–Jun, so the $852 is probably optimistic for deployment — but 2024 shows
  the same summer peak, so the level is seasonal rather than a trend, and the
  April book is not simply "worse".
- **The recommendation excludes 19% of the current book and a forecast 35%.**
  That is a large operational carve-out to justify on 34 churners. The honest
  framing is that we cannot yet tell whether the model helps on corporate, not
  that we know it hurts.

### What changed my mind this session

- I expected the monthly split to be decorative and advised skipping it (D2).
  It turned out to carry the clearest evidence that the value is unstable, so
  it went in. Recorded because it is exactly the kind of pre-commitment that
  should be revisited when the data disagree.
- I predicted that fitting the calibration on September (10.8% base rate)
  would over-correct for a lower-rate test window. Wrong: the raw model
  under-predicts on the test window too, because the test book is more
  corporate and the model scores corporate low.

### Trimming candidates for the two-page limit (need ~450 words out)

1. A1's loss sentence — A3's break-even paragraph says it better (~40 words).
2. A1's corporate and seasonality figures → move to exhibit footnotes (~90).
3. A2's "reading the rows" row-by-row commentary → compress rows 0 and 2,
   which moved least (~120).
4. A2's odds-ratio prose → Exhibit A2c already carries it (~60).
5. A3's final paragraph's post-treatment clause → exhibit footnote (~40).

### Numbers used and where they live

| Number | File |
|---|---|
| AUC 0.644 / 0.404 / 0.641; 4,556 / 408; 860 / 34; 3,696 / 374 | `a2_table.csv` |
| t* = 0.2143, the derivation, both routes | `a3_threshold.txt` |
| $852 / −$78 / +$930 / −$47,736 / $0 / $828; offers and churner counts | `a3_value.csv` |
| SE $572; 1.5 SE from zero | `run.log` (from `value_with_se`) |
| Monthly: 114/81/47 offers, 21.9/33.3/21.3%, $48/$810/−$6 | `a3_by_month.csv` |
| First vs repeat $3.97 / $1.66; Q1 −$2.85; Q4 39.6% vs 27.9% | `a3_offer_quality.csv` |
| Validation: Platt slope 0.788, intercept −0.219, 8 of 10 bins under | `a3_calibration.csv`, `run.log` |
| Curve peak $1,098 at 0.236; raw-score sensitivity $882 | `a3_value_curve.csv`, `run.log` |
| 533 corporate training rows, tenure ≤ 6 | `a1_corporate_segment.csv` |
| Channel odds ratios ~4× | `a2_odds_ratios.csv` |
| Apr–Jun 5.3–7.1% vs Oct–Dec 8.4–9.5% | `a1_base_rate_by_month.csv` |
| 1,294 non-churners with `winback_offer_sent` = 1 | `a1_column_timing.csv` |

Transcript: `sessions/claude-code/a1-session-4.jsonl` and `.txt`.

### What was done

- Pulled session 3 from Windows. **Cross-machine reproducibility verified**:
  re-running everything on the Mac left `a2_table.csv` and all six A1 outputs
  byte-identical. Only `a2_test_scores.csv` moved, by at most 4e-14 in
  `p_churn` (ARM vs x86 floating point), and the *same 203 rows* cleared the
  threshold on both machines, so no dollar figure depends on the laptop.
  `run.log` differs only by Python patch version and path separators.
- Verified A2's partitions against the brief's window table from the data, not
  from reading the code: fitted on 2024-01..2025-06 (18 months), scored on
  2025-10..12 (3 months), 2025-07/08/09 in neither, no month in both.
- `analysis/part1/a3_decision.py` written and added to `run.sh`. Full run is
  ~12 s. Threshold derivation, calibration check and correction, value
  exhibit, monthly split, offer-quality table, value curve and figure.
- `drafts/a3_draft.md`: recommendation, Exhibits A3a-A3d, prose (448 words),
  notes, argue-against list, provenance table, trimming candidates.

### Design decisions made (mine)

- One offer = one member-month (matches the monthly programme and the brief's
  per-offer economics; per-member accounting has no honest answer to "which
  month did the offer happen in", since a churner has only one flagged row).
- Quarter as the reporting period. Monthly split added afterwards once it
  proved informative — I had decided to skip it.
- Priced t* against offer-everyone, no programme, and the analyst's 0.267.
  Declined to score the test window with the analyst's *model*: that is a
  second scoring, and A2 set the norm against it.
- Calibration: checked on the validation month, and corrected there with
  Platt scaling. **The verdict was set from validation evidence before any
  dollar figure existed.** It cost $30.
- Value curve reported (re-reads the same scores, no new scoring).
- Recommendation shape (scope to non-corporate + dollar tripwire) chosen
  before the numbers were computed.
- Declined to add window-compliance assertions to `a2_evaluation.py`: A2 is
  run and answered.

### Numbers produced, with provenance (all from `bash analysis/run.sh`)

| Quantity | Value | File |
|---|---|---|
| Threshold t* | 0.2143 = 18/84, two routes agreeing | `a3_threshold.txt` |
| Value at t*, quarter | $852 (242 offers, 62 to churners, 180 wasted) | `a3_value.csv` |
| Standard error of that total | $572, i.e. 1.5 SE from zero | `run.log` |
| By segment | corporate -$78 (9 offers, 1 churner); other +$930 (233, 61) | `a3_value.csv` |
| Offer to everyone | -$47,736 (4,556 offers, 408 churners) | " |
| No programme | $0 | " |
| At the analyst's 0.267 | $828 (108 offers, 33 churners) | " |
| Monthly at t* | Oct $48 (114 offers, 21.9%); Nov $810 (81, 33.3%); Dec -$6 (47, 21.3%) | `a3_by_month.csv` |
| First vs repeat contact | $3.97 vs $1.66 per offer; 195 vs 47 offers | `a3_offer_quality.csv` |
| Top-quartile over-prediction | claims 39.6%, delivers 27.9% (61 offers) | " |
| Q1 just above t* | 22.2% claimed, 18.0% observed, -$2.85 per offer | " |
| Validation calibration | slope 0.788, intercept -0.219; under-predicts in 8 of 10 bins; val AUC 0.695 | `a3_calibration.csv`, `run.log` |
| Calibration sensitivity | raw scores give $882 on 203 offers | `run.log` |
| Curve peak | $1,098 at threshold 0.236; not selecting cost $264 | `a3_value_curve.csv` |

Hand arithmetic, stated as such: break-even precision = t* = 21.43%, and
value per offer = 84 x (precision - 0.2143); quarter precision 25.6%.

### Findings this session

- **The margin is thin, not the ranking.** Value per offer is $3.52 against a
  break-even precision of 21.4% on a 9% base rate. Two of the three test
  months are at or below break-even; the quarter's $852 is essentially
  November. With 47-114 offers a month those differences are mostly noise,
  which is the finding: the programme sits close enough to zero that ordinary
  variation straddles it.
- **The threshold was not the analyst's main error.** Their grid-searched
  0.267 on honest scores gives $828 against our derived $852. The $19,774 came
  from leaked columns and a shuffled evaluation, not from the cut point.
- **The model overstates the members it selects.** Top-scoring quartile claims
  39.6% and delivers 27.9% — selecting the top of a noisy score. This is why
  the tripwire is a dollar figure, not AUC: AUC can hold while calibration
  drifts and the cut point stops meaning what it meant.
- A fixed threshold is self-regulating *if* the probabilities are honest, so
  a lower April base rate should mean fewer offers rather than worse ones.
  The exposure is miscalibration under drift, not the base rate itself.

   Output-folder question from session 1 still open (`sweep_outputs/` and
   `b3_outputs/` under `analysis/part2/` vs `analysis/outputs/`).

   `drafts/a3_draft.md`; roughly 450 words need to come out.

   material is in `drafts/ai_process_note_draft.md` (session 4 block added).
4. Deadline Thursday 1 October, 6:00 PM Central.

from pathlib import Path
p = Path("drafts/ai_process_note_draft.md"); t = p.read_text()
old = "## Session 3 — (to be added)"
block = """## Session 4 (2026-09-29, macOS) — A3, the targeting decision

**Delegated:** the A3 script (threshold derivation, calibration check and
correction, value exhibit, monthly split, offer-quality table, value curve and
figure); the cross-machine reproducibility check; verifying A2's partitions
against the brief's window table; the A3 draft.

**Changed or rejected:**
- I declined the agent's proposal to add window-compliance assertions to
  `a2_evaluation.py`. A2 is run and its questions are answered; the assertions
  only guard against future edits.
- The agent recommended skipping the monthly split to save words (its "D2"),
  and I agreed. It then turned out to be the clearest evidence that the
  value is unstable — October $48, November $810, December -$6 — so it went
  in after all. A pre-commitment revisited because the data disagreed.
- The agent initially argued that fitting the calibration correction on
  September (10.8% base rate) would over-correct for a lower-rate test
  window. That was wrong and it said so: the raw model under-predicts on the
  test window too, because the test book is more corporate and the model
  scores corporate low.
- I chose one offer = one member-month over per-member accounting, and the
  shape of the recommendation (scope to non-corporate, plus a tripwire)
  before any dollar figure was computed.
- I rejected scoring the test window with the analyst's *model* for a
  like-for-like dollar comparison: it would be a second scoring of the test
  set, and session 3 had already set the norm against that.
- I specified the tripwire in dollars — realised value per offer — rather
  than AUC, after seeing that the model's top-scoring offers claim 39.6% and
  deliver 27.9%, so a ranking statistic can hold steady while the programme
  goes underwater.

**How numbers were checked:**
- Cross-machine: re-ran the whole pipeline on the Mac against outputs
  committed from Windows. `a2_table.csv` and all six A1 outputs byte-identical;
  `a2_test_scores.csv` differed by at most 4e-14 in `p_churn`, and crucially
  the same 203 rows cleared the threshold on both machines, so no dollar
  figure depends on the hardware.
- The threshold was derived two ways in code — 18/(240x0.35) and the general
  form C_FP/(C_FP+C_FN) — with an assertion that they agree, and both read
  the constants from `starter/load.py` rather than being typed in.
- The vectorised value calculation is asserted row by row against the supplied
  `offer_value()` helper, so the economics come from the starter module.
- A2's partitions were verified from the data (months present in each
  partition, no overlap, all 24 accounted for) rather than from reading code.
- The calibration decision was made on validation evidence *before* any dollar
  figure was computed, and it cost $30 — raw scores return $882 against $852
  corrected. Deciding after would have selected the raw scores.
- The figure's annotations disagreed with the exhibit ($834 vs $852) because
  the curve grid did not pass through the derived threshold; caught by reading
  the figure against the table, and fixed by putting t* and 0 into the grid.

**Would still not bet on:** the corporate dollar line (-$78 on nine offers and
one churner); the quartile pattern below the top quartile (~15 churners each);
and that $852 transfers to April-June, which runs a lower base rate and a
book forecast at 35% corporate.

## Session 5 — (to be added)"""
assert old in t
p.write_text(t.replace(old, block))
print("process-note draft updated")

93% of the "readable" transcript is base64 image data from the handout PDF pages I read — so the `.txt` files don't actually serve their purpose. The course sheet says to open your export and read it; a 10 MB wall of base64 fails that.

I'm going to make the renderer show images as labelled placeholders. This is a rendering choice, not an edit to the record: the authoritative JSONL keeps every byte unchanged, and the placeholder states the media type and size.

old = '''RULE = "=" * 78
'''
new = '''RULE = "=" * 78


def describe_image(block):
    """An embedded image, as a labelled placeholder.

    The base64 payload of a screenshot or a rendered PDF page can be a
    megabyte on one line, which makes the readable rendering unreadable --
    in this project's transcripts it was 93% of the file.  Nothing is
    concealed: the media type and the payload size are stated, and the
    authoritative .jsonl beside this file still holds every byte.
    """
    src = block.get("source") or {}
    data = src.get("data", "")
    return "[image omitted from the readable rendering: %s, %s base64 chars; " \\
           "the full payload is in the .jsonl]" % (
               src.get("media_type", "unknown type"), f"{len(data):,}")
'''
assert old in t; t = t.replace(old, new, 1)

old2 = '''    if kind == "tool_result":
        content = block.get("content", "")
        if isinstance(content, list):
            parts = []
            for item in content:
                if isinstance(item, dict) and item.get("type") == "text":
                    parts.append(item.get("text", ""))
                else:
                    parts.append(json.dumps(item, ensure_ascii=False))
            content = "\\n".join(parts)
        return ["[tool_result]", str(content)]
    return ["[%s]" % kind, json.dumps(block, ensure_ascii=False)]'''
new2 = '''    if kind == "image":
        return [describe_image(block)]
    if kind == "tool_result":
        content = block.get("content", "")
        if isinstance(content, list):
            parts = []
            for item in content:
                if isinstance(item, dict) and item.get("type") == "text":
                    parts.append(item.get("text", ""))
                elif isinstance(item, dict) and item.get("type") == "image":
                    parts.append(describe_image(item))
                else:
                    parts.append(json.dumps(item, ensure_ascii=False))
            content = "\\n".join(parts)
        return ["[tool_result]", str(content)]
    return ["[%s]" % kind, json.dumps(block, ensure_ascii=False)]'''
assert old2 in t; t = t.replace(old2, new2, 1)
p.write_text(t); print("renderer updated")

Yes to both, with one correction on each.

## The memo

One document, two sections — not six. Per the brief:

- **§1 to the VP of Membership, Northline Fitness** — max 2 pages of prose, plus Exhibits A1–A3. That's where A1, A2 and A3 live.
- **§2 to the VP of Merchandising Planning, Cascade Outdoor** — max 1 page, plus Exhibits B1–B3.

**The correction: it isn't an amalgamation.** If we staple the three A-drafts together you get a document that reads like a homework answer — A1 opens with "Where the model would have to start from," which is a methods heading, not a memo opening. Course doc §5 is explicit: lead with the recommendation, not the method or the data cleaning. So §1 should open with your A3 recommendation — run it on non-corporate members, $852 not $19,774, with the tripwire — and then work *backwards* through the evidence that justifies it. The A1 baselines and the A2 audit become the support, not the narrative spine. Same for §2 once Part B exists.

The drafts are organised by rubric item so nothing gets lost; the memo has to be reorganised by argument. That's an assembly job, and it's where a chunk of the 450-word trim will come from naturally, since the three drafts currently repeat context for each other.

One thing to sanity-check when we assemble: the brief says "Exhibits A1–A3," and we currently have eight exhibit labels (A1, A2, A2b, A2c, A3a–A3d). Sub-lettering under three top-level numbers is defensible, but four sub-exhibits under A3 is probably one or two too many — A3c (the value table) and the figure are the ones that must be there.

## The process note

Yes, I can draft it — your CLAUDE.md "Drafting" section settles that, and the raw material in [drafts/ai_process_note_draft.md](drafts/ai_process_note_draft.md) already covers all four sessions written from your perspective, because every item in it is a decision you actually made.

**The correction: it's 1,927 words against a one-page limit.** Roughly 500 words survive, so about three-quarters comes out. That's a selection job, and selection is where the grade is — the rubric grades specificity, and "generic notes score zero."

The caution I'd repeat from session 2: this is the one deliverable where a polished draft can work against you. The instructor reads it next to the transcripts, and the failure signal named in the policy is "a transcript showing that a conclusion arrived fully formed and was never questioned, paired with a process note claiming careful validation." Your transcripts show the opposite — you pushed back on the last-row framing, asked whether the leakage evidence was in the run, rejected the assertions, overrode the monthly-split call. So the note should sound like you, and the strongest items are the ones where you corrected me rather than the ones where I built something.

If it helps, the highest-value items across the four sessions, in rough order:

1. You caught that the leakage evidence wasn't reproducible from the run and made it so before it entered a draft.
2. You reversed the monthly-split decision when the data contradicted it.
3. You set the tripwire in dollars rather than AUC, for a reason you can defend.
4. You rejected a second scoring of the test window to keep the A2 norm.
5. Two places I was wrong and you have the record: the September over-correction prediction, and the figure annotation that disagreed with its own exhibit.
